_comment: Written by `showtime new --from-storyboard`: the plan. Scene ids are the <section> ids in index.html and the ## headings in narration.md. `showtime retime --from-voice` reads it to say where the voice outgrew a shot's planned length.

rows.visual: Dark frame, one neuron drawn in thin lines. Type fades in: 1999, "rather far-fetched" quote card. Then a blue pulse hits the cell and it fires (a bright spike travels along it). Last frame (the poster): the blue pulse on the neuron with both lines of type: "light, 'rather far-fetched'" and "Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2026"
rows.brief: Dark frame, one neuron drawn in thin lines. Type fades in: 1999, quote card. Then a blue pulse hits the cell and it fires (a bright spike travels along it). Last frame (the poster): the blue pulse on the neuron with both lines of type: and
onscreen: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2026
rows.narration: In 1999, Francis Crick wrote that light would be the ideal signal for switching neurons, then called the idea rather far-fetched. This week, it won a Nobel Prize.

rows.visual: Citation card with three names (Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, Georg Nagel) and "for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics"; then the four-step roadmap bar slides in at the bottom and stays; step 1 lights
rows.brief: Citation card with three names (Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, Georg Nagel) and ; then the four-step roadmap bar slides in at the bottom and stays; step 1 lights
onscreen: for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics
rows.narration: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel share the prize for discoveries about light-gated ion channels. Four steps, three guesses.

rows.visual: Step 1 lit. A green alga swimming toward a lamp; an eyespot glint; label "about 0.015 mm". On the question line: a timer ring and three answer chips (about the same / about 5x / more than 20x) appear only after the line ends
rows.brief: Step 1 lit. A green alga swimming toward a lamp; an eyespot glint; label "about 0.015 mm". On the question line: a timer ring and three answer chips (about the same / about 5x / more than 20x) appear only after the line ends
rows.narration: Step one: an alga fifteen thousandths of a millimetre wide that swims toward light. Guess: how much faster than your eye does it react?

rows.visual: The alga's response bar against an eye's: "more than 20 times faster"; label "about half a millisecond after light reaches the eyespot"
rows.brief: The alga's response bar against an eye's: "more than 20 times faster"; label "about half a millisecond after light reaches the eyespot"
rows.narration: The Nobel Committee says: over twenty times faster. About half a millisecond after light hits its eyespot, an electrical impulse appears.

rows.shot: 4 the idea and the frog egg
rows.visual: Step 2 lit. One protein drawn as a single piece that catches light and forms a pore in a membrane ("scepticism" speech-bubble); a frog egg with injected genes; blue light on the egg; the pore opens
rows.brief: Step 2 lit. One protein drawn as a single piece that catches light and forms a pore in a membrane ("scepticism" speech-bubble); a frog egg with injected genes; blue light on the egg; the pore opens
rows.narration: Step two: the switch. Peter Hegemann proposed that one protein could catch light and form a channel. People doubted it. Georg Nagel put algal genes into frog eggs, and when light hit, the channels opened.

rows.visual: Step 2 lit. The 4-step channel drawing (light arrives, channel opens, ions flow in, neuron fires) carrying "Chlamydomonas reinhardtii" on the protein; a date card "4 Aug 2004, around 1 a.m."; then a mouse head in outline with a thin optical fibre
rows.brief: Step 2 lit. The 4-step channel drawing (light arrives, channel opens, ions flow in, neuron fires) carrying on the protein; a date card ; then a mouse head in outline with a thin optical fibre
rows.narration: Around one in the morning on 4 August 2004, Edward Boyden saw the first neuron carrying the alga's channel fire in blue light. By 2007, the Committee says, it worked in living mice.

rows.visual: Step 3 lit; permanent label "our toy model: educational demo". A fibre tip in tissue; three coloured glows (blue, yellow, red) spreading at equal size so no answer is shown; question timer ring; chips after the line
rows.brief: Step 3 lit; permanent label "our toy model: educational demo". A fibre tip in tissue; three coloured glows (blue, yellow, red) spreading at equal size so no answer is shown; question timer ring; chips after the line
rows.narration: Step three: our toy model, an educational demo. A thin fibre sends blue, yellow or red light into brain tissue. Guess: which colour reaches deepest?

rows.visual: The depth chart with three curves and the 3 mW per square millimetre line; the answer highlighted; one caveat chip "our model ignores absorption outside blood: read every depth as a rough toy result"; a small card "real fibres: about 100x more light than cells need, because brain scatters it"

onscreen: our model ignores absorption outside blood: read every depth as a rough toy result
real fibres: about 100x more light than cells need, because brain scatters it
rows.narration: Red: {R1}. But our model ignores absorption outside blood, so read every depth as rough.

rows.visual: The warming chart: continuous versus pulsed light; a thermometer chip "2019 study: 0.2 to 2 degrees C"; the chart marked "our toy model"
rows.brief: The warming chart: continuous versus pulsed light; a thermometer chip "2019 study: 0.2 to 2 degrees C"; the chart marked "our toy model"
rows.narration: Tissue turns absorbed light into heat: a 2019 study measured 0.2 to 2 degrees Celsius of warming. In our toy model, pulsing the light cuts it: {R2}.

rows.visual: The 3D scatter animation: neurons lighting up as power rises to the toy heat limit (label "one assumed limit: 1 degree C"); the counter hidden; question timer ring; answer chips appear only after the line ends
rows.brief: The 3D scatter animation: neurons lighting up as power rises to the toy heat limit (label "one assumed limit: 1 degree C"); the counter hidden; question timer ring; answer chips appear only after the line ends
rows.narration: How many neurons can one degree of warming recruit? Guess: hundreds, thousands, or tens of thousands?

rows.narration: In our toy model: blue, about {R3a}; yellow, about {R3b}.
